ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
British physicist J.J. Thomson believed that cathode rays were streams of charged particles. To confirm this, he conducted a series of experimental studies starting from 1890. In the experiments, the charged particles emitted from the cathode K formed a fine beam of rays through small holes A and B, passing through the space between two parallel metal plates D1 and D2, and reaching a fluorescent screen with a scale at the right end. By observing the position of the fluorescence produced by the rays, the trajectory of the rays could be studied. During the experiment, an accelerating voltage was applied between the anode A and the cathode K, and a deflection voltage of magnitude U was applied between D1 and D2, where the potential of D1 was lower than that of D2. When a uniform magnetic field in the positive y-direction with a magnetic induction strength of B was applied between D1 and D2, a bright spot appeared at P1; keeping other conditions unchanged, after removing the uniform magnetic field, the stream of charged particles hit the lower side of P1, and the angle between the direction of the velocity and the line connecting the small holes A and B was θ (the gravitational force on the charged particles was negligible).

1. What is the speed of the charged particle when it enters D1 and D2?
2. What is the specific charge of a charged particle?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows a cathode K on the left and two small holes/diaphragms A and B that collimate the beam. The beam then travels horizontally to the right along the x-direction through the space between two parallel plates: D1 is the upper plate and D2 is the lower plate. The vertical separation of the plates is marked d, with the z-axis vertical and the y-axis drawn obliquely. A fluorescent screen is on the right, with P1 near the middle and P2/P3 below/above it. The potential markings show the upper plate side is negative/lower potential and the lower plate side is positive/higher potential. The deflecting plate region has length a along the beam direction as used in the problem method. Reasoning: The electric field magnitude between the plates is E = U/d. In the run with the magnetic field present, the spot is at P1; when the magnetic field is removed, the beam hits below P1. Thus, in the crossed-field run, the magnetic deflection must cancel the electric deflection. Using magnitudes, qE = qvB, so v = E/B = U/(dB). For the electric-only run, the charged particle moves horizontally through the plates with speed v, so the time spent between the plates is t = a/v. Its transverse acceleration magnitude is (q/m)E = qU/(md), taking q/m as the magnitude of the specific charge. Therefore the transverse exit velocity is v_z = (qU/(md))(a/v). The exit angle θ satisfies tanθ = v_z/v = qUa/(m d v^2). Solving gives q/m = d v^2 tanθ/(Ua). Substituting v = U/(dB) gives q/m = U tanθ/(a d B^2).
